course: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer – Professional (AIP-C01)
part_title: Lab 10 — Debug Agent Tool Loops, Contracts, Permissions and Retries
review_basis: Original WebPs 55–61 visually reviewed with detailed trace events, action-group envelopes, Lambda/IAM views and idempotency/approval controls.

scenes.title: Scenario and agent tool architecture
scenes.narration: The synthetic order-lookup agent keeps calling the same tool for order A one zero four without producing a reliable answer. Follow the architecture from the user to the Bedrock Agent planner, action group OrderLookupTool, Lambda backend and Orders API. The action-group schema expects an orderId string. The tool result returns to the agent, which decides whether to finish, retry or take another action. In the right trace illustration, tool calls repeatedly start and then fail; the sample event detail reports a ValidationError for an unexpected response format. Open the Bedrock agent Test or Trace view with tracing enabled for this sandbox and record the exact tool arguments, result envelope, error code and correlation ID. Distinguish the tool's genuine backend failure from a valid backend response wrapped incorrectly for the action-group schema. The learner's first task is not to increase maximum agent iterations. It is to locate the first error and prove why the agent receives no usable observation. We will then verify permissions and schema, repair the backend or response contract, and restrict repeated actions.

scenes.title: Inspect trace and repeated tool calls
scenes.narration: In the Bedrock Agents Trace tab, filter the session for the same order identifier and step through timestamps. The sample first invokes orderLookup with orderA104, receives an upstream five hundred four timeout, retries the same tool, and then receives a response referring to orderA103. The latter is a contract and data-integrity failure: a tool cannot satisfy the request by returning a different order. Match every invocation with its corresponding result and correlation ID. Inspect arguments, response status, order identifier and underlying Lambda logs before assuming the agent reasoning is defective. The right-hand Lambda permissions panel reminds you that Bedrock must have permission to invoke the function, while Lambda separately needs downstream access. If the error is a timeout, inspect backend health and timeout budget; if the result is an unexpected order, inspect request mapping and response validation. Keep a record of the first failed attempt so a later retry does not obscure the original fault. Repeated identical calls are a signal that the orchestrator needs bounds, but they do not explain the backend cause by themselves.

scenes.title: Validate arguments and result contract
scenes.narration: This slide zooms in on the structured Bedrock action-group envelope. Trace the user request for order A104 through application routing into an action group named OrderLookup with function lookupOrder. The illustrative request includes messageVersion one point zero and parameters with an orderId field. On the response side, the function response must carry the expected actionGroup and function names and a responseBody containing the text result in the agreed representation. The sample response's text body is a JSON string containing orderId A104 and status SHIPPED. Validate the serialized structure with the exact action-group type your deployment uses rather than copying one illustrative payload blindly. A raw HTTP statusCode and body from an ordinary Lambda proxy integration is not automatically a valid Bedrock action-group return. In the simulator, compare the tool schema, required argument names and result envelope against the actual tool invocation. Reject mismatched order IDs and malformed responses before the agent uses them as observations. When this contract passes, re-run the original order query and check that one correct result is enough to end the loop.

scenes.title: Diagnose Lambda and downstream permissions
scenes.narration: The trace shown here includes an AccessDeniedException for lambda InvokeFunction, which is a separate failure branch from a malformed response. First identify the actual agent, Lambda function, account and source ARN from the trace. Then open Lambda Permissions and inspect the resource-based policy that lets the Bedrock service principal invoke that specific function, ideally scoped to the corresponding agent ARN. Next check the Lambda execution role's authorization to call the downstream Orders API or database. The slide illustrates a read-only DynamoDB permission as one possible backend policy, not a blanket permission requirement for every order lookup. Follow the exact error: an invoke denial needs an invocation-policy correction; a downstream database denial needs its own narrowly scoped role access. The sample CLI add-permission command is for an appropriately authorized, scoped repair, not for unrestricted public invocation. Also inspect the function result against the action-group response schema. Apply the minimum supported policy or contract change and test again while retaining correlation IDs and a rollback record. Do not broaden permissions to fix unrelated timeouts or data mapping mistakes.

scenes.title: Repair tool behavior and version routing
scenes.narration: The repair process has five stages: fix the Lambda response contract, verify scoped invocation and downstream permissions, prepare an updated Bedrock Agent draft, test it, and route the application to a validated alias. The diagram's repair result envelope includes a status, list of changes and a working alias, but it is an application-defined control structure rather than an AWS console setting. Review the code and permission changes independently. Run tests against a draft that returns the requested order ID with the correct schema, and ensure permission and timeout errors are handled without repeated unrestricted calls. The sample application log shows a working draft prepared, eight of eight tests passing, and previous routing retained for rollback. Do not route production traffic to a candidate alias before confirming the correct version and readiness. Keep the last known-good alias and a reversible release plan. Retry limits, loop detection, citation buffering and approval rules belong in your orchestration controls unless your chosen framework provides explicit supported equivalents.

scenes.title: Bound loops retries and side effects
scenes.narration: Look at the central application orchestrator controlling three types of actions: read data, compute, and write data. The sample policy limits a request to three total tool calls, a thirty-second deadline and two attempts for a retryable failure, with repeated-argument detection. These numbers illustrate a bounded design rather than universal recommendations. Configure the actual retry budget so an upstream timeout cannot create an infinite model-tool loop. Detect when the same tool is called with the same arguments and no new evidence. For operations that change state, use idempotency keys so retries do not duplicate writes, and require trusted human or system approval for critical modifications. The sample log shows a knowledge-base read, a compute step, then a DynamoDB write after approval, ending within the deadline. A model deciding to call a tool is not an authorization event on its own. Enforce approval, permissions and transaction semantics outside model-generated text. Validate that a retry of the same approved write does not create another update and that exhausted budgets yield a controlled failure message.

scenes.title: Verify success denied timeout and invalid-input paths
scenes.narration: The last slide combines four fixtures that must remain distinct. For success, ask for order A104, verify the tool receives the correct structured orderId, and confirm that the response contains the same order and expected status. For access denial, remove only the test fixture's scoped invocation permission and ensure the trace records the authorization failure rather than retrying indefinitely. For a timeout, simulate an unavailable downstream Orders API and verify the agent records the timeout and stops or retries within defined bounds. For invalid input, omit the required orderId and expect validation before an unsafe tool call. The trace illustration shows tool arguments, invocation results, errors and a correlation ID; use them to diagnose which branch occurred. Before release, update the approved agent version and alias, test both success and negative paths, and remove temporary overly broad policies or test order records. The lab is complete when there is one correct answer for the good request and predictable, contained behavior for every failure case.
